common_name: Crown Jewels Hardy Hibiscus (Purple-Leaved White with Red-Eye Perennial Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container-grown crowns in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Crown Jewels is a compact Fleming Brothers hybrid of Hibiscus moscheutos and the Gulf Coast native scarlet swamp hibiscus, bearing purple-black maple-shaped foliage and round white flowers with a bold dark red eye.

directions: Grow in consistently moist to wet, fertile soil in full sun, since both of its parent species are wetland natives that perform best with reliable water through the growing season. Crown Jewels carries deeply cut, dark purple to near-black maple-like leaves inherited from its coccineus parentage, setting off 6-inch round white flowers with a vivid dark red central eye that appear in steady succession from midsummer through early fall. Its more compact, densely branched habit compared to older large-leaved moscheutos hybrids makes it a good fit for smaller beds or rain garden margins where the scale of standard dinner-plate hibiscus can overwhelm. As with all hardy hibiscus, the plant dies to the ground each winter and is often one of the last perennials to break dormancy in spring, so mark the crown location to avoid disturbing it before new shoots appear.

common_name: Robert Fleming Hardy Hibiscus (Velvety Deep Red Perennial Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container-grown crowns in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Robert Fleming is a compact, bushy Fleming Brothers introduction prized for its velvety, deep red 8-10 inch flowers with a darker red eye.

directions: Plant in moist to wet, fertile soil in full sun and water deeply during dry spells, since this hardy hibiscus naturally grows at pond edges and low wet ground. Robert Fleming produces huge, velvety, deep red flowers with a darker red throat that open in continuous succession from midsummer into fall against green, maple-shaped foliage, and its comparatively bushy, well-branched habit keeps the plant tidier than many older large-flowered hardy hibiscus. Named for one of the Fleming brothers whose decades-long Nebraska breeding program also produced Kopper King and Crown Jewels, it shares their reliable cold hardiness and vigor. Cut the dead canes back to the ground in late winter and expect new growth to emerge late in spring, often not until most other perennials have leafed out.

common_name: Cherry Cheesecake Hibiscus (White with Magenta-Tipped Petals and Red Eye Hardy Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Cherry Cheesecake bears extra-large 8-inch white flowers with magenta-tipped, ruffled petals radiating from a cherry-red eye, part of the Summerific hardy hibiscus breeding series.

directions: Grow in moist, fertile soil in full sun, keeping the root zone reliably watered through summer to support the enormous flower display this cultivar is known for. Cherry Cheesecake opens thick, heavily ruffled, overlapping white petals brushed with magenta at the tips and veined out from a bold cherry-red eye, with buds forming continuously up the stems so the plant stays in near-constant bloom from midsummer to fall even though each individual flower lasts only a day. The leathery, dark green, maple-shaped foliage carries a faint purple-gray overlay that complements the flower color. This is one of the larger-growing Summerific introductions, so give it room at the back of a bed or along a pond margin, and cut the dead stems to the ground after frost each winter.

common_name: Candy Crush Hibiscus (Bubblegum Pink with Dark Eye Hardy Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Candy Crush bears bright bubblegum-pink flowers up to 8 inches across with a dark burgundy-black eye, on a vigorous, well-branched Summerific hardy hibiscus plant.

directions: Plant in moist to wet, fertile soil in full sun and irrigate during dry stretches, since hardy hibiscus flowers largest and most abundantly with consistent moisture. Candy Crush produces vivid bubblegum-pink blooms with heavily ruffled, overlapping petals and a dark, near-black eye that creates strong contrast, flowering profusely from midsummer through early fall on a vigorous, quick-filling plant. The green, maple-like foliage stays clean and full-bodied through the season on this fast-growing selection, making it a strong choice for a quick, bold color statement in a new bed. Like other hardy hibiscus, it should be cut back to the ground after the foliage is killed by frost, and gardeners should expect it to emerge later in spring than most perennials.

common_name: Edge of Night Hibiscus (Jet-Black Foliage Bubblegum Pink Compact Hardy Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Edge of Night pairs the darkest foliage yet seen in the Summerific series with large bubblegum-pink flowers on one of the most compact hardy hibiscus available.

directions: Grow in moist, fertile soil in full sun, or even in a bog planting near a water feature, since this cultivar tolerates consistently wet ground better than most garden perennials. Edge of Night carries jet-black foliage — among the darkest of any hardy hibiscus introduced to date — with contrasting green calyxes and red petioles, setting off large 7-8 inch bubblegum-pink flowers with darker pink veining that give the blooms a dramatic three-dimensional look. Its notably compact, wide-spreading habit keeps the plant shorter than most large-flowered hardy hibiscus while still producing an abundant, season-long floral display from midsummer into late fall. Cut the plant to the ground after frost each winter and expect new shoots to emerge later in spring than most other perennials in the bed.

common_name: Spinderella Hibiscus (Pinwheel-Patterned White and Pink Hardy Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Spinderella bears large 8-inch flowers with a distinctive pinwheel pattern of darker bubblegum-pink edges fading to light pink toward the overlapping petal base.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, watering deeply during hot, dry spells to sustain the plant's enormous flower size. Spinderella produces large, overlapping petals with darker bubblegum-pink margins that fade sideways into pale pink toward their overlap, creating a distinctive pinwheel pattern across each bloom, set against a dense, dark green foliage mound. Flowering runs continuously from midsummer into early fall, with individual flowers lasting a single day but replaced daily by new buds along the stems. Give this large-growing selection ample room at the back of a border or along a pond edge, and cut the dead stems down to the crown once frost has killed the foliage each winter.

common_name: Evening Rose Hibiscus (Near-Black Foliage Hot Pink Hardy Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Evening Rose pairs near-black foliage with hot pink 8-inch flowers, giving strong color contrast typical of the darkest-leaved Summerific hardy hibiscus cultivars.

directions: Grow in moist, fertile soil in full sun and keep the root zone consistently watered, since hardy hibiscus flowers are largest and most numerous when the plant never dries out. Evening Rose carries near-black, slightly glossy, oval leaves that provide a dramatic backdrop for its heavily puckered, hot pink flowers, which can reach 8 inches across and open in steady succession from midsummer through fall. Its upright, mounding habit stays tidy and well proportioned for a mid-border planting, and the dark foliage remains attractive from spring emergence until frost even when the plant is not in bloom. As with other hardy hibiscus, cut the canes to the ground after winter dieback and expect growth to resume later in spring than most companion perennials.

common_name: Ballet Slippers Hibiscus (White with Pink-Edged Petals and Red Eye Hardy Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Ballet Slippers bears large 7-inch ruffled white flowers kissed with pink at the petal edges and centered with a brilliant red eye.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, providing supplemental water during dry periods to keep flower production strong. Ballet Slippers opens ruffled, overlapping white petals with a soft blush of pink along the edges and a brilliant red central eye, held above bright green foliage on an upright, mounding plant loaded with buds from tip to base. It is an indeterminate bloomer that flowers continuously from mid to late summer through the first hard frost, offering one of the longer bloom windows among the large-flowered hardy hibiscus. Cut the canes to the ground once winter kills the foliage, and mulch the crown in colder parts of its range to protect against extreme cold snaps.

common_name: Coconut Cream Hibiscus (Creamy White-Yellow with Red Eye Hardy Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Coconut Cream bears large creamy white flowers with a tinge of yellow and a bold red eye, set against deep olive-green foliage with burgundy highlights.

directions: Grow in moist, fertile soil in full sun and irrigate through dry spells to support this cultivar's oversized flower display. Coconut Cream produces large, creamy white flowers with a soft yellow undertone and a bold red central eye, opening in continuous succession over many weeks from midsummer into fall, well after many other perennials have finished blooming. The heart-shaped, deep olive-green leaves carry burgundy highlights that make the foliage attractive even between flushes of bloom. Its upright habit fits well toward the back of a mixed perennial border or along the edge of a rain garden, and the plant should be cut to the ground each winter after frost kills the top growth.

common_name: Cookies and Cream Hibiscus (Compact White-Flowered Dark-Foliage Hardy Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Cookies and Cream is an exceptionally compact hardy hibiscus with frilly white flowers held above dark burgundy-black foliage.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, keeping the root zone consistently moist through summer heat. Cookies and Cream carries overlapping, frilly, bright white petals with a slight pink blush on the reverse and light yellow stamens, opening as dinner-plate-size blooms up to 6-7 inches across against dark burgundy-black foliage that provides dramatic contrast even before flowering begins in August. Its exceptionally compact and sturdy habit makes it one of the more manageable hardy hibiscus for smaller gardens or foundation plantings where taller cultivars would overwhelm the space. Cut the plant back to the ground once frost ends the season, and expect it to re-emerge later in spring than most other perennials nearby.

common_name: Garnet Globes Hibiscus (Compact Deep Garnet-Red Hardy Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Garnet Globes forms a tidy, rounded mound topped with large deep garnet-red flowers, one of the most compact hardy hibiscus introductions available.

directions: Grow in moist, fertile soil in full sun, watering during dry stretches to keep the compact plant flowering at its best. Garnet Globes produces frilly, pleated, deep garnet-red petals with a darker central eye on flowers up to 7 inches across, held against deep olive-green, glossy foliage that stays lush through the display. Unlike many hardy hibiscus that can become tall or sprawling, this selection maintains a tight, mounded, sphere-like habit that holds its shape without staking, making it well suited to smaller beds, containers, or as a structural accent along a walkway. Cut the canes to the ground after frost kills the top growth each winter, and expect new shoots to emerge later in spring than most companion perennials.

common_name: Head Over Heels Passion Hibiscus (Bright Pink with Crimson Center Compact Hardy Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Head Over Heels Passion bears vibrant pink flowers with a bold crimson center against deep burgundy foliage on a compact, upright plant.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, since this cultivar adapts well to wet, low-lying ground and even tolerates some soil salinity, an asset in Gulf Coast landscapes. Head Over Heels Passion opens big, vibrant pink flowers with a bold crimson center and slightly crepe-textured, overlapping petals against foliage that emerges purple in spring, turns green with purple tones by summer, and finishes gold in fall. Its fast-growing, compact, upright habit and strong resistance to leaf scorch, leaf spot, and powdery mildew make it a lower-maintenance choice than many older hardy hibiscus. Remove dead canes in early spring rather than fall, since the crown is prone to rot if cut too early, and expect it to be one of the last perennials in the bed to break dormancy.

common_name: Head Over Heels Blush Hibiscus (Light Pink Darkening to Bright Pink Compact Hardy Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Head Over Heels Blush bears light pink flowers that darken toward the outer petal edges, set against burgundy foliage on a compact, upright plant.

directions: Grow in moist, fertile soil in full sun, taking advantage of this cultivar's tolerance for wet sites and some soil salt, which suits low spots or coastal-influenced Gulf gardens. Head Over Heels Blush opens light pink flowers that deepen to bright pink toward the outer edge of each petal, creating a soft two-tone effect against burgundy-tinted foliage, and it flowers from late spring through early autumn on a compact, upright, fast-growing plant. It is notably one of the last perennials in the garden to break dormancy in spring, sometimes staying bare into early summer, so avoid disturbing the crown when neighboring plants have already leafed out. Remove dead canes in early spring rather than cutting back in fall, and feed once yearly with a slow-release fertilizer to support its vigorous seasonal growth.
